items.title: Butch Miles interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 9, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I think I got slaughtered on that thing when I was working with Gerry Mulligan and a quartet back in the 80s, and I did a number of gigs with him and the big band

ctx.x: Is it possible to be specific about one part of your playing that is different?

I don’t state the beat so hard anymore. I don’t pound at you. I’ve learned to get up off that bass drum and use that as a musical voice more often but I still use it as the bottom line in connection with a good walking bass player, not so much to beat somebody up with but just to give a little bit more support to. And use my feet, both feet, as other voices so that I try to think of now, I try to think in more musical terms, percussive terms. I think I got slaughtered on that thing when I was working with Gerry…
Was that a group without a chordal instrument?

items.title: Butch Miles interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: You know we’ve been good, close friends for a number of years and he was always remarkable to work with

ctx.x: Yeah, it sure did. But working with Brubeck and the whole Brubeck clan was just absolutely delightful. And then, after that, it’s been very notable. I’ve worked off and on for a few years with Lena Horne, who is one of my favorite all-time people in the world, not only just as an entertainer, but as a person, I love her. I’ve worked with Gerry Mulligan off and on for a couple of years, fascinating experience, I really dig Gerry. You know we’ve been good, close friends for a number of years and he was always…
your statement, it’s quick. And once again it was the machine, it had to be like that. Otherwise you could have 18 anarchists up there on stage.
